On 11 and 13 May 1998 India set off five nuclear devices under the desert at Pokhran in Rajasthan. Pakistan answered with tests of its own on 28 and 30 May. South Asia now had two declared nuclear powers.

India had tested one device in 1974 and called it peaceful (see Smiling Buddha). Both countries then built the means to make bombs without testing. Pakistan's programme, begun by Zulfikar Ali Bhutto after the defeat of 1971, used enrichment technology brought from Europe by the engineer A. Q. Khan.

A new government under Atal Bihari Vajpayee ordered the tests weeks after taking office. The team, led by Abdul Kalam and R. Chidambaram, worked at night and in army uniform to hide from American satellites. India said it needed the weapons because of China.

Pakistan's prime minister was pressed hard by the United States not to reply and offered aid if he held back. Seventeen days later Pakistan tested in the Chagai hills of Balochistan.

Both countries were put under sanctions, which were lifted within a few years. They fought the Kargil War the next summer. India has promised never to use nuclear weapons first; Pakistan has not. A 2008 agreement with the United States brought India back into world nuclear trade.
sum: On 11 and 13 May 1998 India set off five nuclear devices under the desert at Pokhran in Rajasthan. Pakistan answered with tests of its own on 28 and 30 May. South Asia now had two declared nuclear powers.
